analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and pays for it by taxing high earners' full income.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on May 20, 2025 and has sat there since, with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would expand Social Security: a higher minimum benefit for people who worked low-wage jobs their whole lives, extra benefits for those who have been on the rolls for 16+ years, and child benefits extended to age 26 for full-time college students. To pay for it, the bill phases out the cap on wages subject to Social Security taxes (currently about $176,100), so by 2035 all earnings are taxed, and raises the payroll tax rate from 6.2% to 6.5% for workers and employers. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has remained with no action and no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low earners get a minimum benefit scaled to the poverty line based on years worked; beneficiaries 16+ years on the rolls get a gradually increasing boost up to 5%; children of disabled, retired, or deceased workers who attend college full-time keep benefits to age 26; and increases are ignored by other assistance programs so no one loses food or housing aid for getting a larger Social Security check [S2][S3]. High earners also gain somewhat because their newly taxed earnings above the cap count toward their benefits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-earning and long-term Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum Social Security benefit for lifetime low earners, scaling with years worked (including years spent caring for young children), up to a benchmark tied to the federal poverty guideline.

Adds a benefit increase for people who have been on Social Security for 16 or more years, reaching 5% of a reference benefit after 20 years — aimed at the oldest beneficiaries who have seen their benefits erode.
Lets children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers keep receiving benefits through age 26 while a full-time college student.
Ensures any benefit increase does not count as income for other federal or federally funded assistance programs, so higher Social Security checks cannot cost someone food or housing benefits.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and employers. Social Security payroll taxes rise from 6.2% to 6.5% on everyone's wages over six years, and the cap on taxed earnings (about $176,100 in 2025) is phased out so that by 2035 all earnings are taxed — a direct tax increase on income above the current cap for roughly the highest earners, plus a matching cost for their employers [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax rate rises from 6.2% to 6.5% for every worker and employer over six years, a visible pay-cut-adjacent cost for all wage earners, and a cost that employers may partly pass on in lower wages.

High earners and small business owners with income above the cap face substantial new taxes: by 2035 every dollar of earnings above today's threshold would be newly taxed, even though only a 3% benefit formula factor applies to those earnings above the cap, meaning many top contributors pay in more relative to what they get back.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and targeted at people with modest means: higher minimum and long-duration benefits, and longer student-child benefits. The costs are also real and specific: a payroll tax increase shared by workers and employers, and new tax liability for earnings above the current cap. The design addresses the common objection that taxing high earners without crediting them is unfair by crediting those earnings toward benefits, but the burden on employers could nudge some toward wage suppression or automation at the margin. On balance, the bill shifts financing toward the highest earners to strengthen a program most people depend on.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died in committee.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 20, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action has been taken since the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote is listed in the action history.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill itself, but the richest households avoided the new payroll taxes above the wage cap that the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners spared new payroll taxes

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over Social Security
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on May 20, 2025 and took no further action — no hearing or markup is listed.

against.name: High-earner and business interests
against.what_they_did: Groups representing businesses and high earners have historically opposed applying the Social Security payroll tax above the wage cap, and no member of either party cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no coalition formed on either side; the record shows only the sponsor's action.

industries.industry: High earners above the Social Security wage cap (roughly the top 6% of earners)
industries.note: Currently earnings above $176,100 are exempt from the 6.2% Social Security payroll tax; the bill phases that exemption out completely by 2035 and raises the rate. This is where the money for benefit increases comes from.
The employer share of the Social Security tax rises from 6.2% to 6.5% over six years, raising labor costs for every business, small and large.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since referral, the bill is unlikely to advance. Bills increasing payroll taxes on high earners rarely get hearings in a closely divided Congress, and Ways and Means took no step toward a markup.
